paras: The attempted lynching of David Bell took place at Marshall, Madison County, North Carolina, in April 1888, when a mob of about one hundred men gathered at the county jail to lynch Bell, who was held on a charge of assaulting a married woman. The sheriff removed Bell from the jail by a ruse and took him to Asheville, and Bell was later tried, convicted and sentenced to death. A Knoxville wire story about the attempt ran in papers as far away as Kansas and Arkansas.

According to the Asheville Citizen, Bell worked for T. J. Tilson of Ivy, in Madison County, and was accused of attempting to rape Mrs. Tilson on the night of April 5 while her husband was away. Her brother and others went after Bell and caught him the next morning. The paper's correspondent added that he did not know "whether he is dead or not," a remark the Citizen called "significant." None of the reports gives the race of Bell or of Mrs. Tilson.

A Knoxville dispatch dated April 9 said Bell had been arrested at Marshall "last night" and lodged in jail. That morning, by the same account, a mob of "more than 100 desperate men" gathered around the jail intending to lynch him. The sheriff got Bell away by what the dispatch called "a clever ruse" and took him to Asheville, where he was "safely caged." No violence by the mob and no arrests of its members were reported.

Bell was tried that summer before a jury, which received the case on a Saturday afternoon and returned a verdict of guilty on the following Monday. Judge Boykin sentenced him to be hanged on September 20, and a motion for appeal was entered. No report of the appeal's result or of an execution appears in the coverage.

All coverage came from white papers. The Asheville Citizen headlined its first report "Dastardly Outrage" and stated the charge as fact, and its comment on the correspondent's uncertainty hinted that the pursuers might have killed Bell. The Knoxville wire story, printed by the Wichita Eagle on April 10 under the headline "Almost a Lynching," called Bell "the fiend" and the mob "desperate men," and gave credit to the sheriff for saving his prisoner. Four days later the Forrest City Times in Arkansas reduced it to one sentence among unrelated "Telegraphic Brevities."
The trial and sentence were reported by the Asheville Citizen and reprinted in the Charlotte Democrat's "State News" column on August 10 under the heading "Sentenced to Be Hung."

The dates differ between the local and wire accounts. The Asheville Citizen, printing on April 7, placed the alleged assault on the night of April 5 and Bell's capture the next morning, while the Knoxville dispatch of April 9 put his arrest at Marshall on the previous night. The local report is closer to the events, but only the wire describes the mob at the jail, so the date of the attempt rests on that dispatch alone.
